To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The sympathetic preganglionic neurons in the lumbar spinal cord of rats are organized in a topographic map that is similar to the topographic organization of the somatic sensory map; (2) This topographic organization is maintained in the sympathetic preganglionic outflow; and (3) Sympathetic preganglionic neurons receive convergent sensory inputs from the viscera and somatic tissues.

the reflex control of the bladder, and the reflexes that control the sympathetic nerves that supply the bladder.

the role of the sympathetic nerves in the regulation of bladder function and the control of micturition.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lumbar sympathetic preganglionic neurones have afferent input from the pelvic viscera, and that this afferent input is mediated by the pelvic nerve.
the lumbar sympathetic nerves contain fibres that respond to activation of vesico-somatic afferent fibre in the Aγ range.
the lumbar sympathetic preganglionic neurons to the inferior meseneric ganglion receive excitatory input from the pelvic afferent fibers in the Aγ-delta range.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sympathetic nervous system is not a single system, but a collection of different systems, each of which has a unique function in the body.
the lumbar plexus is a complex network of nerves, which is responsible for a variety of functions in the lower body.

the sympathetic outflow from the spinal cord is not a simple, linear reflex pathway, but rather is modulated by a complex network of interneurons that can be influenced by descending inputs from the brain.
